**(Benefit)**

The Prophet's (ﷺ) saying to ʿUmar, "And what makes you know? Perhaps God looked upon the people of Badr and said: Do whatever you wish, for I have forgiven you," has puzzled many people. Its apparent meaning permits them every action and gives them the choice of whatever they wish, and that is impossible. A group of scholars, including Ibn al-Jawzi, said: The intended meaning of His words "do" (iʿmalū) is not the future tense but the past, and the sense is: "Whatever deed you did, I have forgiven it."

He said: Two things indicate this:

First, if it were in the future tense, its response would be His words, "I will forgive you" (fasa-aghfiru lakum).

Second, it would be an unrestricted permission for sins, and there is no justification for that.

The reality of this answer is: "By this expedition I have forgiven you what preceded of your sins." But it is weak on two counts:

First, the word "do" (iʿmalū) rejects it, for it is in the future tense, not the past.

Second, His words "I have forgiven you" do not require that "do" be like it. His words "I have forgiven" confirm that forgiveness will occur in the future, like His words, "The command of God has come" (﴿أتى أمر الله﴾) and "Your Lord has come" (﴿وجاء ربك﴾), and their like.

Second, the hadith itself refutes it. Its occasion was the story of Hatib and his spying on the Prophet (ﷺ), and that sin occurred after the Battle of Badr, not before it. This was the cause of the hadith, so it is certainly intended by it.

What we think about this, and God knows best, is that this is an address to a people whom God, glory be to Him, knew would not abandon their religion but would die in Islam, and that they might commit some of the sins that others commit. Yet He, glory be to Him, does not leave them persisting in them. Rather, He grants them sincere repentance, seeking forgiveness, and good deeds that erase the trace of that. Their being singled out for this, rather than others, is because it has been established regarding them that they are forgiven. This does not prevent the forgiveness from being obtained through causes that are carried out by them, just as it does not necessitate that they neglect the obligations out of confidence in forgiveness. Had the forgiveness been obtained without continuing to perform the commands, they would not have needed prayer, fasting, pilgrimage, zakat, or jihad afterward, and this is impossible. Among the most obligatory of obligations is repentance after sin. The guarantee of forgiveness does not necessitate abandoning the causes of forgiveness.

A parallel to this is His saying in another hadith: "A servant committed a sin and said: My Lord, I have committed a sin, so forgive me. He forgave him. Then he remained as long as God willed, then committed another sin and said: My Lord, I have committed a sin, so forgive me. He forgave him. Then he remained as long as God willed, then committed another sin and said: My Lord, I have committed a sin, so forgive me. God said: My servant knows that he has a Lord who forgives sin and takes account for it. I have forgiven My servant, so let him do whatever he wishes." There is no unrestricted permission in this, nor any license from Him, glory be to Him, for him to do forbidden things and crimes. It only indicates that He forgives him as long as he is in that state: when he sins, he repents. The singling out of this servant is because it is known that he does not persist in a sin, and that whenever he sins he repents. The ruling covers everyone whose state is like his, but that servant is assured of this, just as the people of Badr were assured of it. Likewise, everyone whom the Messenger of God (ﷺ) gave glad tidings of Paradise, or informed that he was forgiven, was not understood by him or by any other Companion to be an unrestricted license for him to commit sins and disobedience, or to be lax about abandoning obligations. Rather, these people were more diligent, cautious, and fearful after the glad tidings than they were before them, like the ten who were testified to be in Paradise.

Abu Bakr was very cautious and fearful, and so was ʿUmar. They knew that the unrestricted glad tidings were bound by their conditions, by continuing upon them until death, and bound by the absence of their impediments. None of them understood from that unrestricted statement a permission to do whatever deeds they wished.

**(Section)**

The Messenger of God (ﷺ) ordered the people to prepare for the campaign, and he ordered his family to equip him. Abu Bakr entered upon his daughter ʿAʾisha, may God be pleased with her, while she was moving some of the equipment of the Messenger of God (ﷺ). He said: "My daughter, did the Messenger of God (ﷺ) order you to equip him?" She said: "Yes, so prepare." He said: "Then where do you think he intends to go?" She said: "No, by God, I do not know."

Then the Messenger of God (ﷺ) informed the people that he was setting out for Mecca. He ordered them to strive and prepare, and said: "O God, cut off the spies and the news from Quraysh until we surprise them in their lands."

So the people prepared.

Hatib ibn Abi Balta'a wrote a letter to Quraysh informing them of the Messenger of God's (ﷺ) march toward them. Then he gave it to a woman and set a reward for her if she delivered it to Quraysh. She put it in the braids of her hair and set out with it. Then news from heaven came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) about what Hatib had done. He sent ʿAli and al-Zubayr, and other than Ibn Ishaq said: he sent ʿAli, al-Miqdad, and al-Zubayr. He said: "Go until you reach Rawdat Khakh, for there is a woman with a letter to Quraysh." So they set out, their horses racing with them, until they found the woman at that place. They made her come down and said: "Do you have a letter?" She said: "I have no letter." They searched her saddle-bag and found nothing. ʿAli, may God be pleased with him, said to her: "I swear by God that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) did not lie, nor did we lie. By God, you will bring out the letter, or we will strip you bare." When she saw his earnestness, she said: "Turn away." He turned away, and she untied the braids of her hair and brought out the letter from them. She handed it to them, and they brought it to the Messenger of God (ﷺ). There it was:

"From Hatib ibn Abi Balta'a to Quraysh, informing them of the Messenger of God's (ﷺ) march toward them."

The Messenger of God (ﷺ) summoned Hatib and said: "What is this, Hatib?" He said: "Do not hasten against me, O Messenger of God. By God, I believe in God and His Messenger. I have not apostatized or changed. But I was a man attached to Quraysh, not one of their own kind, and I have family, kin, and children among them, and I have no tribal relatives among them to protect them. Those with you have relatives who protect their families. So when I lost that, I wanted to make a favor with them by which they would protect my relatives." ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab said: "Let me strike his neck, O Messenger of God, for he has betrayed God and His Messenger, and he has become a hypocrite." The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "He has witnessed Badr. And what makes you know, O ʿUmar? Perhaps God looked upon the people of Badr and said: Do whatever you wish, for I have forgiven you." Then ʿUmar's eyes overflowed, and he said: "God and His Messenger know best."

Then the Messenger of God (ﷺ) went on, fasting, and the people were fasting too, until when they reached al-Kudayd, which is what people call Qudayd today, he broke his fast and the people broke their fast with him.

Then he went on until he halted at Marr al-Zahran, which is the valley of Marr. With him were ten thousand. God concealed the news from Quraysh, so they were in fear and awaiting. Abu Sufyan used to go out to spy for news, so he went out with Hakim ibn Hizam and Budayl ibn Warqa', spying for news. al-ʿAbbas had set out before that with his family and dependents, a Muslim emigrant. He met the Messenger of God (ﷺ) at al-Juhfa, and it was said beyond that. Among those who met him on the road was his paternal cousin Abu Sufyan ibn al-Harith and ʿAbd Allah ibn Abi Umayya. They met him at al-Abwa', and they were his paternal cousin and his paternal aunt's son. He turned away from them because of the severe harm and mockery he had suffered from them. Umm Salama said to him: "Let not your paternal cousin and your aunt's son be the most wretched of people toward you." ʿAli said to Abu Sufyan, as Abu ʿUmar related: "Go to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) from the front of his face and say to him what the brothers of Joseph said to Joseph: (﴿By God, God has certainly preferred you over us, and we were indeed sinners﴾ [Yusuf 12:91]), for he does not accept that anyone be better than him in speech." Abu Sufyan did this, and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said to him: (﴿No reproach will be upon you today; God forgives you, and He is the most merciful of the merciful﴾ [Yusuf 12:92]).

Abu Sufyan recited verses of poetry, among them:

"By your life, when I bear a banner
to make the horses of al-Lat overcome the horses of Muhammad,
I am like the traveler by night, bewildered, whose night grew dark,
so this is my time, when I am guided and find the way."

"A guide other than myself guided me,
and directed me to God, having driven away every driven one."

The Messenger of God (ﷺ) struck his chest and said: "You have driven me away from every expulsion." His Islam was good after that.

It is said that he did not raise his head to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) from the time he became Muslim, out of shame before him. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) loved him, and testified to him that he would enter Paradise, and said: "I hope he will be a successor to Hamza." When his death approached, he said: "Do not weep for me, for by God I have not uttered a sin since I became Muslim."

When the Messenger of God (ﷺ) halted at Marr al-Zahran, he halted there at night. He ordered the army, and they lit fires, so ten thousand fires were lit. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) placed ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, may God be pleased with him, in charge of the guards.

al-ʿAbbas mounted the white mule of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and went out seeking, perhaps he might find some woodcutter, or someone who would inform Quraysh, so that they would come out seeking safe conduct from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) before he entered it by force. He said: "By God, as I was riding it, I heard the speech of Abu Sufyan and Budayl ibn Warqa', and they were returning, and Abu Sufyan was saying: I have never seen such fires or such an army as tonight." He said: Budayl said: "By God, these are the Khuza'a, whom war has stirred up." Abu Sufyan said: "The Khuza'a are too few and too humble to have these fires and this army." He said: "I recognized his voice, so I said: Abu Hanzala?" He recognized my voice and said: "Abu al-Fadl?" I said: "Yes." He said: "What is wrong with you, may my father and mother be your ransom?" I said: "This is the Messenger of God (ﷺ) among the people. Woe to Quraysh, by God!" He said: "Then what is the plan, may my father and mother be your ransom?" I said: "By God, if he gains the upper hand over you, he will surely strike your neck. So mount behind me on this mule, until I bring you to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and seek safe conduct for you from him." So he mounted behind me, and his two companions returned. He said: "So I brought him, and whenever I passed by a fire of the Muslims, they said: Who is this? When they saw the mule of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and me on it, they said: The uncle of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) on his mule. Until I passed by the fire of ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, and he said: Who is this? He stood up to me, and when he saw Abu Sufyan behind me on the animal's rump, he said: Abu Sufyan, the enemy of God? Praise be to God who has brought you within reach without a covenant or a pact." Then he ran toward the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and I spurred the mule, and it outran him, and I dismounted from the mule and entered upon the Messenger of God (ﷺ). ʿUmar entered upon him too and said: "O Messenger of God, this is Abu Sufyan, so let me strike his neck." I said: "O Messenger of God, I have given him protection." Then I sat beside the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and took hold of his head, and I said: "By God, no one will confide in him tonight besides me." When ʿUmar kept insisting about him, I said: "Gently, O ʿUmar. By God, if he were one of the men of the clan of ʿAdi ibn Kaʿb, you would not have said such a thing." He said: "Gently, O al-ʿAbbas. By God, your Islam was more beloved to me than the Islam of al-Khattab would have been, had he become Muslim. I only did it because I knew that your Islam was more beloved to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) than the Islam of al-Khattab." Then the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Take him, O al-ʿAbbas, to your lodging, and when morning comes, bring him to me." So I went, and when morning came, I went early with him to the Messenger of God (ﷺ). When the Messenger of God (ﷺ) saw him, he said: "Woe to you, Abu Sufyan! Has the time not come for you to know that there is no god but God?" He said: "May my father and mother be your ransom, how forbearing you are, how generous, and how kind! I thought that if there were a god with God other than Him, it would have availed me something by now." He said: "Woe to you, Abu Sufyan! Has the time not come for you to know that I am the Messenger of God?" He said: "May my father and mother be your ransom, how forbearing you are, how generous, and how kind! As for this, there is still something in my soul about it until now." al-ʿAbbas said to him: "Woe to you! Become Muslim and testify that there is no god but God and that Muhammad is the Messenger of God, before your neck is struck." So he became Muslim and bore witness to the testimony of truth.

al-ʿAbbas said: "O Messenger of God, Abu Sufyan is a man who loves glory, so grant him something." He said: "Yes. Whoever enters the house of Abu Sufyan is safe, and whoever closes his door upon himself is safe, and whoever enters the Sacred Mosque is safe."

al-ʿAbbas was ordered to hold Abu Sufyan at the narrow point of the valley, by the nose of the mountain, until the armies of God passed by him and he saw them. He did so, and the tribes passed by under their banners. Whenever a tribe passed by him, he said: "O al-ʿAbbas, who is this?" I said: "Sulaym." He said: "What have I to do with Sulaym?" Then another tribe would pass by him, and he would say: "O al-ʿAbbas, who are these?" I would say: "Muzayna." He would say: "What have I to do with Muzayna?" Until the tribes were exhausted; every tribe that passed by him asked me about them, and when I informed him of them, he said: "What have I to do with the sons of so-and-so?" Until the Messenger of God (ﷺ) passed by him in his green battalion, in which were the emigrants and the helpers, of whom nothing could be seen but the eyes of iron. He said: "Glory be to God! O al-ʿAbbas, who are these?"

I said: "This is the Messenger of God (ﷺ) with the emigrants and the helpers." He said: "No one has the strength or power against these." Then he said: "By God, O Abu al-Fadl, the kingdom of your nephew has become great this morning." I said: "O Abu Sufyan, it is prophethood." He said: "Yes, then." I said: "Hasten to your people."

The banner of the Ansar (the Helpers) was with Sa'd ibn 'Ubadah. When he passed by Abu Sufyan, he said to him: "Today is the day of slaughter. Today what is sacred will be violated. Today Allah will humiliate Quraysh."

When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ drew level with Abu Sufyan, Abu Sufyan said: "O Messenger of Allah, did you not hear what Sa'd said?" He asked: "And what did he say?" Abu Sufyan replied: "Such and such." 'Uthman and 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf said: "O Messenger of Allah, we are not secure that he may have a surge of power among Quraysh." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Rather, today is a day on which the Ka'bah will be exalted, today is a day on which Allah will honour Quraysh."

Then the Messenger of Allah ﷺ sent for Sa'd, took the banner (liwa') from him and gave it to his son Qays. He regarded the banner as not having left Sa'd, since it had passed to his son. Abu 'Umar said: It is also narrated that when the Prophet ﷺ took the banner (rayah) from him, he gave it to al-Zubayr.

Abu Sufyan went on until he reached Quraysh, and he cried out at the top of his voice: "O assembly of Quraysh, this is Muhammad, who has come to you with a force you cannot withstand. Whoever enters the house of Abu Sufyan is safe."

Then Hind bint 'Utbah stood up to him, seized his moustache and said: "Kill this fat, base, thin-shanked old greybeard! Evil is the vanguard of a people!" He said: "Woe to you! Let this woman not deceive you about yourselves, for there has come to you what you cannot withstand. Whoever enters the house of Abu Sufyan is safe, and whoever enters the mosque is safe." They said: "May Allah destroy you! What good will your house do us?" He said: "And whoever closes his door upon himself is safe, and whoever enters the mosque is safe." So the people dispersed to their homes and to the mosque.

The Messenger of Allah ﷺ proceeded and entered Makkah from its upper part, where a tent (qubbah) was pitched for him. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ ordered Khalid ibn al-Walid to enter from its lower part. He was in command of the right wing (al-mujannabah al-yumna), which included Aslam, Sulaym, Ghifar, Muzaynah, Juhaynah, and tribes from among the tribes of the Arabs. Abu 'Ubaydah was in command of the infantry (al-rajjalah) and the unarmed (al-hussar), that is, those who had no weapons with them. He said to Khalid and those with him: "If any of Quraysh confront you, mow them down until you meet me at al-Safa." No one confronted them except that they were put to sleep (i.e., struck down).

Ibn al-Qayyim, al-Tafsir al-Qayyim, on Surah 60, verses 8–9:

When [Allah] forbade, at the beginning of the surah, the Muslims from taking the disbelievers as allies (awliya') and from cutting off affection between them and the disbelievers, some of them imagined that showing kindness (birr) to them and doing good (ihsan) to them was part of taking them as allies and of affection. So Allah, glorified is He, made clear that this is not of the kind of alliance (muwalah) that is forbidden, and that He did not forbid this; rather it is of the goodness (ihsan) that He loves and is pleased with, and that He has prescribed (kataba) upon every thing. What is forbidden is only taking the disbelievers as allies (tawalli) and conveying affection to them (al-ilqa' ilayhim bil-mawaddah).

Ibn al-Qayyim, al-Tafsir al-Qayyim, on Surah 60, verses 8–9:

When [Allah] forbade, at the beginning of the surah, the Muslims from taking the disbelievers as allies (awliya') and from cutting off affection between them and the disbelievers, some of them imagined that showing kindness (birr) to them and doing good (ihsan) to them was part of taking them as allies and of affection. So Allah, glorified is He, made clear that this is not of the kind of alliance (muwalah) that is forbidden, and that He did not forbid this; rather it is of the goodness (ihsan) that He loves and is pleased with, and that He has prescribed (kataba) upon every thing. What is forbidden is only taking the disbelievers as allies (tawalli) and conveying affection to them (al-ilqa' ilayhim bil-mawaddah).

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 60, verse 10:

[Section: On his ruling ﷺ regarding fulfilling the covenant with his enemy, and regarding their envoys, that they are not to be killed or imprisoned, and on rejecting (al-nabdh) the one with whom he has a covenant on equal terms when he fears a breach of the covenant from him]

It is established from him that he said to the two messengers of Musaylima the Liar, when they said: "We say that he is the Messenger of Allah": "Were it not that messengers are not killed, I would have killed you both."

It is also established from him that he (said to Abu Rafi', whom Quraysh had sent to him, and who wanted to remain with him and not return to them: "I do not break a covenant, and I do not hold back messengers. Rather, return to your people, and if what is in your soul now remains, then return.")

It is also established that he "returned Abu Jandal to them, in accordance with the covenant that was between him and them, that he would return to them whoever came to him from them as a Muslim." But he did not return the women. Subay'a al-Aslamiyya came as a Muslim, and her husband went out seeking her. Then Allah, Mighty and Majestic, revealed: ﴿O you who have believed, when believing women come to you as emigrants, examine them. Allah is most knowing of their faith. And if you know them to be believers, then do not return them to the disbelievers﴾, and the rest of the verse.

The Messenger of Allah ﷺ then made her swear that she had not been driven out except by desire for Islam, and that she had not left because of some wrongdoing she had committed among her people, nor out of hatred for her husband. She swore, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ gave her husband his dowry, and did not return her to him.

This, then, is his ruling, which accords with the ruling of Allah, and nothing has come that abrogates it whatsoever.

As for whoever claims that it is abrogated, he has nothing but a bare assertion, and the explanation of this has already been given in the account of al-Hudaybiyya.

(Section)

"The pledge of allegiance in the time of the Messenger of God ﷺ was by handshake, and the pledge of the women was by speech. The noble hand of the Prophet ﷺ never touched the hand of a woman he did not own. He would say to whoever pledged allegiance to him: 'I have pledged you,' or 'I pledge you,' concerning hearing and obedience, in hardship and ease, in what is pleasant and what is disliked," as in the two Sahihs (al-Sahihayn) from Ibn Umar: "We used to pledge allegiance to the Messenger of God ﷺ to hear and obey, and he would say: 'As far as you are able.'" And in Sahih Muslim from Jabir: "On the day of al-Hudaybiyah we were fourteen hundred, and we pledged allegiance to him while Umar held his hand under the tree. We pledged to him that we would not flee, and we did not pledge him to death."

And in the two Sahihs from Ubadah ibn al-Samit, who said: "We pledged allegiance to the Messenger of God ﷺ to hear and obey in hardship and ease, in what is pleasant and what is disliked, and over being given preference over us, and that we would not dispute the command with its people, and that we would speak the truth wherever we were, fearing in God the blame of no blamer."

Also in the two Sahihs from Junadah ibn Abi Umayyah, who said: "We entered upon Ubadah ibn al-Samit while he was ill, and we said: 'Relate to us, may God set you right, a hadith by which we may benefit, which you heard from the Messenger of God ﷺ.' He said: 'The Messenger of God ﷺ called us and we pledged allegiance to him. Among what he took from us was that we pledged to him to hear and obey in what is pleasant and what is disliked, in our hardship and our ease, and over being given preference over us, and that we would not dispute the command with its people,' and he said: 'Except that you see clear disbelief (kufr bawah) with proof from God concerning it.'"

And in the two Sahihs from Aishah, she said: "When believing women emigrated to the Messenger of God ﷺ, he would test them with the saying of God the Exalted: ﴿O Prophet, when believing women come to you pledging allegiance to you that they will not associate anything with God, nor steal, nor commit adultery, nor kill their children...﴾ [al-Mumtahanah: 12] to the end of the verse."

Aishah said: "Whichever of the believing women affirmed this had affirmed the test. When they affirmed this in their words, the Messenger of God ﷺ would say to them: 'Go, for I have pledged you.' By God, the hand of the Messenger of God ﷺ never touched the hand of a woman at all; he only pledged them by speech."

"Aishah said: By God, the Messenger of God ﷺ never took the pledge from women except with what God commanded him, and the palm of the Messenger of God ﷺ never touched the palm of a woman at all. When he took their pledge he would say to them: 'I have pledged you,' by speech alone."

This is the Prophetic pledge concerning which God the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿Indeed, those who pledge allegiance to you, they are only pledging allegiance to God. The hand of God is over their hands. So whoever breaks his oath, breaks it only to his own detriment, and whoever fulfills what he has covenanted with God, He will give him a great reward﴾ [al-Fath: 10].

And He said concerning it: ﴿Certainly God was pleased with the believers when they pledged allegiance to you under the tree﴾ [al-Fath: 18].
